decisions.title: Agent State Control Plane
decisions.decision: cancellAI evolves from a cleaner into a local-first, cross-platform, provider-agnostic Agent State Control Plane. The product sequence is storage control plane first, cross-platform Guardian second, broader AI-developer hygiene only where it remains directly tied to agent-generated state.
decisions.rationale: Vendor-native cleanup will improve and commoditize narrow deletion. Cross-provider visibility, governance, prevention, and lifecycle control remain structurally underserved.
implications: Provider adapters are replaceable edges, not the product core.
The product boundary is agent-generated local state, not generic system cleanup.
Cross-platform architecture is required from the core model onward.

decisions.title: Wedge market sequence
decisions.decision: Start obsessively with power developers and AI-native builders, design the architecture to expand to mainstream developers, and preserve a natural path to team and enterprise governance.
decisions.rationale: Power users experience the problem earliest and most intensely while providing the best feedback surface for a developer-first product.
implications: CLI/TUI quality is a first-order product concern.
Zero-config experiences are added without weakening advanced controls.
Fleet features must not compromise the local OSS core.

decisions.title: Progressive value promise
decisions.decision: Enter with safe reclaim plus complete visibility, evolve into prevention, then into full lifecycle governance of agent state.
decisions.rationale: Immediate reclaim solves a concrete pain while observability creates a durable path beyond cleanup.
implications: SEE and RECLAIM precede PREVENT and GOVERN.
Every roadmap phase must preserve prior explainability.

decisions.title: Adaptive authority with quarantine-first
decisions.decision: Authority progresses from Observe to Recommend to Quarantine to Govern to Autopilot. Quarantine is preferred when technically possible. Authority depends on confidence, artifact type, reversibility, provider capability, and user policy.
decisions.rationale: Power should increase only when safety evidence supports it.
implications: Autopilot is never a global bypass.
Unknown or protected artifacts remain Observe Only.
Irreversible actions require stronger gates than reversible ones.

decisions.title: Multidimensional artifact model
decisions.decision: The internal model is artifact-centric and multidimensional across machine, project, provider, artifact, and session. Primary UX is machine/project-centric with immediate alternative views.
decisions.rationale: A single provider hierarchy reproduces the fragmentation cancellAI is intended to overcome.
implications: Project attribution is evidence-based and may remain Unattributed.
No aggressive inference is allowed merely to make dashboards look complete.

decisions.title: Three-tier knowledge model
decisions.decision: Classification uses Verified Knowledge, Observed Evidence, and Inferred Signals. Every conclusion carries provenance and confidence; inference may improve recommendations but cannot silently elevate destructive authority.
decisions.rationale: Intelligence must remain explainable and safe under provider drift.
implications: Every classified artifact has evidence provenance.
Low-confidence classifications are non-destructive.
AI assistance, if introduced, remains advisory in destructive paths.

decisions.title: Local authority, federated intelligence
decisions.decision: The full local core works offline. Optional network intelligence may distribute signed/versioned provider knowledge and receive privacy-minimized opt-in signals. Cloud knowledge can inform but never directly authorize deletion.
decisions.rationale: Local-first execution preserves trust while a network knowledge plane can improve compatibility across a fast-moving ecosystem.
implications: No account is required for local product functionality.
Knowledge updates are separated from software updates.
Remote control never bypasses local safety invariants.

decisions.title: Open local ecosystem, commercial fleet plane
decisions.decision: Scanner, safety kernel, artifact model, provider SDK/adapters, CLI/TUI, quarantine, Guardian, and local policy engine remain open source. Future commercial value lives in multi-machine governance, organization visibility, audit aggregation, and enterprise integration.
decisions.rationale: A filesystem tool must be inspectable by individual developers; monetization should come from coordination rather than removing local capability.
implications: OSS must remain independently useful and complete on one machine.
Commercial boundaries are architectural, not arbitrary feature locks.

decisions.title: CLI and TUI are first-class clients
decisions.decision: CLI and TUI share one domain engine and contain no safety or domain logic of their own. Guardian and Desktop are later clients of the same core.
decisions.rationale: Power users need scriptability and rich exploration without semantic drift between interfaces.
implications: All operations expose structured engine APIs.
CLI JSON contracts are stable and versioned.
A TUI-generated plan and CLI-generated plan must be semantically equivalent.

decisions.title: Spec-first clean migration to Rust
decisions.decision: Fix only P0 safety defects in the Python implementation, extract an executable behavioral contract and adversarial fixtures, freeze Python as the reference implementation, then build a Rust core and switch only after differential parity and explicit documented divergences.
decisions.rationale: A rewrite without a behavioral oracle would throw away proven safety knowledge; indefinitely extending the monolith would undermine the target architecture.
implications: Python v1 is a reference, not the target architecture.
No large new feature belongs in the Python monolith.
Differential testing is a release gate for the migration.

decisions.title: Composite formal safety model
decisions.decision: Every AgentArtifact has Risk Class, Reversibility, Knowledge Confidence, Activity State, and Authority Ceiling. Effective authority is the minimum allowed by user policy, artifact ceiling, confidence, reversibility, provider capability, and trust.
decisions.rationale: A scalar SAFE/UNSAFE label cannot capture a destructive lifecycle tool's real constraints.
implications: Safety limits are first-class data, not scattered conditionals.
UNKNOWN, ACTIVE, PROTECTED, PARTIAL SCAN, STALE PLAN, PATH ESCAPE, and IDENTITY CHANGED states are non-destructive.

decisions.title: Multidimensional lifecycle plus event history
decisions.decision: Current lifecycle is modeled independently across Activity, Residency, Protection, and Integrity. Significant transitions are append-only events. Purged artifacts retain only contentless tombstones needed for audit and aggregate intelligence.
decisions.rationale: State such as ORPHANED and PINNED must coexist without forcing one ambiguous status field.
implications: Lifecycle transitions are explicit domain operations.
Purge does not require forgetting that space was reclaimed.

decisions.title: Capability-based provider ecosystem
decisions.decision: Providers declare granular capabilities. Simple integrations may be manifest-only; complex integrations use native adapters. Trust levels are Built-in Verified, Community Verified, Local Custom, and Untrusted, and directly bound authority.
decisions.rationale: Provider support must be evolvable and honest rather than all-or-nothing.
implications: Manifest knowledge never implies destructive trust by itself.
Claude Code and Codex are reference providers; Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, and OpenCode follow.

decisions.title: Declarative hierarchical policy with deterministic resolution
decisions.decision: Human-readable policies are hierarchical and compiled into typed internal policy. Deterministic constraint resolution produces an Effective Policy with complete explanation. Precedence is Safety Invariants > Artifact Authority Ceiling > Provider/Trust Capability > Explicit Pin/Protection > Specific Policy > General Policy > Default.
decisions.rationale: Configuration cannot become a backdoor around the safety kernel.
implications: Policy decisions are reproducible.
An explain-policy path is part of the public contract.

decisions.title: Predictive pressure-aware Guardian with bounded autonomy
decisions.decision: Guardian separates detection, decision, and authority. It may use capacity, velocity, behavioral anomaly, structural anomaly, local baselines, and pressure states, but cannot self-escalate beyond Effective Policy and safety ceilings.
decisions.rationale: The product should prevent runaway storage before disk exhaustion without turning prediction into destructive permission.
implications: Forecasts are advisory evidence, not authorization.
Guardian can be intelligent while remaining operationally constrained.

decisions.title: Bounded local memory
decisions.decision: Persistence has three layers: reconstructible Current State, append-only Operational Event Ledger, and aggregated Analytical Memory. Retention and compaction are automatic and cancellAI has a strict self-budget. State is contentless by default and ephemeral inspection is supported.
decisions.rationale: The product must remember enough to improve without becoming another storage leak.
implications: Filesystem/provider state remains authoritative.
Local reset deletes cancellAI state only and inventory can be rebuilt.

decisions.title: Signed canonical releases and multi-channel distribution
decisions.decision: Canonical releases produce signed/attested artifacts, checksums, SBOM, provenance, and a release manifest. Distribution is multi-channel. Knowledge updates are separate from software updates. Installation source is tracked. Stable, beta, and nightly channels have different authority ceilings; WSL is modeled as a distinct environment.
decisions.rationale: A destructive local tool needs a verifiable supply chain and cross-platform distribution without granting experimental builds stable-level authority.
implications: The release factory becomes evidence-driven.
Package-manager and direct-install upgrades respect their original installation source.

decisions.title: Evidence-gated development and independent verification
decisions.decision: Every work item has Change Risk Level CR0-CR4, separate Definition of Done and Definition of Safe, an independent verifier, evidence-driven functional/safety/compatibility/operability gates, and an owner-visible Safety Verdict for high-risk changes.
decisions.rationale: Passing tests alone is not adequate evidence for software that can irreversibly mutate user data.
implications: Executor and verifier roles are separate and may rotate.
Verifier works primarily from specification, criteria, invariants, and threat cases rather than executor reasoning.
CR4 work cannot become release-eligible without explicit safety evidence.

decisions.title: Custom provider roots require validated structure and explicit intent
decisions.decision: Superseded by PD-020. A non-default root was to be mutated when it contained content-validated provider markers and the operator passed --allow-custom-root.
decisions.rationale: Independent review produced a lookalike satisfying both conditions. Structural evidence is forgeable, so it cannot be positive provider identity, and operator intent cannot supply the missing proof when the failure mode is intent based on a wrong value.
implications: Relocated provider roots require an explicit flag in scripts and cron entries.
Refusal is visible and non-destructive: exit code 4 naming the missing condition.
Provider-native identity remains the target for the Rust core once the provider capability contract exists.

decisions.title: Custom provider roots are inspection-only in the Python reference
decisions.decision: Only the provider's own default directory may be mutated by the Python reference. A relocated CODEX_HOME/CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR is fully inspectable and never deleted from or written to.
decisions.rationale: SI-002 requires proof that a directory belongs to the provider. Everything the filesystem can show is forgeable, and an operator flag supplies intent rather than proof. Positive identity needs the provider capability contract that E05 defines and this reference does not have.
implications: Operators who relocated a provider root lose clean and configure until the Rust core ships provider-native identity.
The structural fingerprint remains as reported information and is documented as non-authoritative.
--allow-custom-root is removed rather than kept as a switch that cannot make the operation safe.

decisions.title: Closing an epic cuts a release
decisions.decision: An epic reaching done produces a version tag and everything that follows it: version bump, cut changelog section, updated Homebrew formula, GitHub release, and a committed release evidence packet. scripts/release.py automates the sequence and scripts/check_process.py refuses a done epic without release evidence naming it.
decisions.rationale: E00 closed with every P0 defect repaired and none of it released, while the shipped formula still pointed at a build whose protected-name constants were documentation rather than a barrier. Finished work that does not reach users is not a neutral state: the gap between verified and released grows until releasing becomes its own project.
implications: Version numbers move at the cadence of epics rather than of user-visible feature changes.
The release is verified at the commit it was cut from, by re-running every gate at the tag.
A release requires two commands because the archive checksum cannot exist before the tag does.

decisions.title: Review is per epic and bounded to two rounds
decisions.decision: Superseded by PD-024. Review was bounded to two rounds per epic, with findings surviving round two becoming backlog work items rather than triggering a third round.
decisions.rationale: E00 ran three review rounds with no rule that would ever stop it; the loop ended because the owner stopped it, not because the process had a completion criterion. Per-story review also made the reviewer re-read overlapping code while the epic could not converge.
implications: A second round can miss what a third would have caught; E00's third round found a real defect. The risk is accepted explicitly and mitigated by converting survivors into scheduled work.
Each review round is larger, covering a whole epic rather than one story.
Story status ready_for_review now means waiting for the epic's review round, not requesting an individual one.

decisions.title: Cross-epic story dependencies must not form a review-closure cycle
decisions.decision: E16-S02 ("Signed knowledge bundle format") depended on both E16-S01 and E17-S01. Combined with PD-021 (closing an epic cuts a release, requiring every story done) and PD-022 (an epic reviews only once every story is ready_for_review), this was a hard cycle: E16-S02 could not reach ready_for_review without E17-S01 being done; E17-S01 could not be done until E17 closed; E17 could not close while E17-S07 stayed blocked on E16-S05 being done; E16-S05 could not be done until E16 closed; and E16 could not close while E16-S02 stayed unfinished. E16-S02's dependency on E17-S01 is removed, leaving only E16-S01 - the release manifest's knowledge_compatibility field (E17-S01, project/schemas/release_manifest.schema.json) already exists as a committed schema fact E16-S02 can read and design against without needing that story's own status to advance further.
decisions.rationale: A pairwise cross-epic dependency is fine in isolation; PD-021/PD-022's all-stories-together closure rule turns a *cycle* of such dependencies (E16 to E17 and E17 back to E16) into a structural deadlock no amount of implementation work can resolve. The fix removes one edge of the cycle rather than relaxing PD-021/PD-022, since the all-together closure rule is the one earning its keep (a smaller release/review surface) and the removed edge was not load-bearing (E16-S02 needs the already-shipped schema shape, not E17-S01's story status).
implications: Backlog authors adding a cross-epic story dependency should check whether the reverse direction already exists (directly or transitively) before committing it - PD-021/PD-022 together turn any such cycle into a deadlock, not just a scheduling inconvenience.

E17-S07's own dependency on E16-S05 (rather than E16-S02, which is what its "trusted signed knowledge" downgrade mechanism actually needs) is left as-is by this decision - it is a separate, non-blocking accuracy question about which E16 story E17-S07 should cite, not itself a cycle, and is not resolved here.

decisions.title: Review stops on measured yield, not on a round count
decisions.decision: Another review round is required while a round rejects 10% or more of the stories it judges. Two rounds whose findings do not overlap escalate to the owner rather than closing, because a zero overlap bounds nothing. Three rounds remains a cost ceiling that scripts/check_process.py enforces, and reaching it is an owner decision recorded as such, not an automatic close.
decisions.rationale: PD-022 fixed the number at two without evidence that two is where yield falls off. The process measurement in E25-S01 says it is not a constant: E00's second round rejected more than its first (100% against 86%) and its two rounds found disjoint sets, which leaves Lincoln-Petersen undefined; E20's second round collapsed to zero. E00 needed a third round, got one by exception, and that round found more defects. A stopping rule the measurement can support replaces a constant nobody measured.
implications: An epic whose first round rejects little closes after one round, which PD-022 did not allow.
An epic whose rounds disagree entirely stops being a process question and becomes an owner decision.
ADR-0025 carries the full argument; this entry is the register's record of it, and PD-022 is superseded rather than edited so the earlier rule stays readable.

decisions.title: E14's epic-level dependency on E13 is not load-bearing and is removed
decisions.decision: E14 ("Predictive Guardian Intelligence") declared a coarse epic-level dependency on E13 ("Self-Budget and Local State Ownership") in addition to E10. E13-S04 and E13-S06 are ready_for_review pending an independent reviewer round, which holds the whole E13 epic at in_progress and, through the epic-level edge, blocked E14 from starting at all. What E14 actually reads from E13 is already committed and done: E14-S01 and E14-S03 each declare their own story-level dependency on E13-S03 (done), and E12-S04 - which shares this same review bottleneck - depends on E13-S02 (done) directly rather than on the E13 epic. The coarse E14->E13 epic edge added nothing E14's own story-level dependencies did not already state more precisely, so it is removed from project/epics/E14.json, leaving E14->E10. Owner-authorized 2026-09-20 to unblock E14 and E12-S04 while E13-S04/S06 await review.
decisions.rationale: Same pattern as PD-023: a coarse epic-level dependency edge can hold up work that a story-level dependency already gates correctly and more precisely. E14's actual prerequisite is the specific E13 output its stories read (E13-S03's local-state/self-budget model), not E13's full closure, which additionally requires E13-S04/S06 to clear independent review - a review-availability constraint unrelated to whether E14 can safely start.
implications: E14-S01 and E14-S03's own dependency on E13-S03 remains the real, enforced gate; nothing about E14's technical prerequisites changed.
E13 still needs E13-S04/S06 to pass independent review before the epic itself can close and cut its own release evidence - this decision does not close E13 or substitute for that review.
Backlog authors should check, as PD-023 already asks, whether a coarse epic-level dependency is standing in for a narrower story-level one before adding or keeping it.

decisions.title: E17's epic-level dependency on E06 points the wrong way and is replaced by the epics its stories consume
decisions.decision: E17 ("Verifiable Supply Chain and Distribution") declared a coarse epic-level dependency on E06 ("Rust CLI Parity and Cutover") in the original 2026-08-27 roadmap. No E17 story depends on any E06 story: their story-level dependencies are E02-S02, E16-S05, E17-*, E20-S03 and E26-S01. The only real edge between the two epics runs the other way - E06-S04 (the canonical engine switch) waits on E17-S07 (incident containment), because a cutover needs the supply-chain and containment machinery, not the reverse. Held as declared, the edge makes E17 unclosable until E06 closes, and E06 cannot close until E06-S04 does, which itself needs E17-S07: every E17 story can be done while the epic stays open for a reason no story states. The E17->E06 edge is replaced by E17->[E02, E16, E20, E26], the epics its stories actually read. Owner-authorized 2026-09-23 as part of reducing open work to E06-S04 alone.
decisions.rationale: Same pattern as PD-023 and PD-025: a coarse epic-level edge standing in for, and here contradicting, the precise story-level graph. E17 releases describe supply-chain machinery that exists and is verified independently of whether the Rust CLI is canonical; E06-S04 remains the gate that decides when that machinery ships the Rust engine as the default.
implications: E06-S04 keeps its own dependency on E17-S07; the cutover still cannot happen before incident containment is done and independently verified.
E17 may close, and cut its release, once its own stories are done - this decision does not close E17 or substitute for its review.
E18's dependency on E17 is unchanged and now reflects a real closure order rather than a transitive wait on the cutover.

decisions.title: E18's epic-level dependency on E17 is not load-bearing and is removed
decisions.decision: E18 ("Remote Targets and Fleet Boundary") declared epic-level dependencies on E16 and E17 in the original roadmap. None of its stories reads anything E17 produced: E18-S01 depends on E16-S02 (the signed-envelope primitive its remote requests reuse), and E18-S02/E18-S03 depend only on their predecessors in E18. E18's three stories are done and its independent review closed at round 3 with a 0% yield. The E17 edge therefore only holds a finished, reviewed epic open behind E17-S07, whose closure is waiting on an owner decision about independent verification rather than on anything E18 needs. The edge is removed from project/epics/E18.json, leaving E18->E16. Owner-authorized 2026-09-23 as part of reducing open work to the cutover.
decisions.rationale: Same pattern as PD-023, PD-025 and PD-026: a coarse epic-level edge that no story-level dependency backs. The fleet boundary E18 defines (signed remote intents, local-only authority, the open node protocol) is independent of the supply-chain and incident-containment work E17 carries.
implications: E18 may close and cut its release now that its own stories are done and reviewed.
E17 stays open until E17-S07 has an independent Safety Verdict or the owner decides otherwise; nothing in E18 changes that.
A future fleet story that distributes containment notices (E17-S07's wire format) must declare its dependency on E17-S07 explicitly at story level.

decisions.title: The independent-review pool is Codex or OpenCode on a pinned non-Anthropic model; pre-review never counts
decisions.decision: Codex credit limits stopped independent review for hours at a time. The owner accepted (2026-09-24) a second reviewer: OpenCode driving one pinned non-Anthropic model through OpenRouter, preferring free models. Every review, from either reviewer, runs through scripts/review_round.py, which reviews committed HEAD in a fresh worktree, names the record, attributes the model from the session's stream log rather than from the record, refuses Anthropic models as self-review, and limits and imports only the paths a reviewer may change. A second tier, the advisory pre-review (<EPIC>-PRE-REVIEW-<n>.md), lets a cheap model read work before a formal round; it is never a round, never a verdict, never counted toward the per-story cap or ADR-0025's yield rule, and cannot move a story.
decisions.rationale: Independence here is the first IEC 61508 rung: a different model family from the executor. Any non-Anthropic family satisfies it; the risk a second reviewer adds is attribution (which model actually reviewed) and scope (what it changed), and the harness makes both mechanical instead of trusting the reviewer's own record. Free models trade quality and availability for cost, so a pre-review tier spends them where a miss is cheap.
implications: A record whose stream log names a second model or any Anthropic model is not an independent round.
scripts/process_metrics.py reports independent rounds per reviewer family and lists pre-reviews apart from rounds.
The owner's cap of two independent reviews per story counts formal rounds from either reviewer; pre-reviews do not count.
The end-of-project retrospective revisits the pool with measured per-family yield.
